props.title: It Takes Two
props.initialSlug: Identical strangers plot to unite their caregivers

sections.content: **It Takes Two** (1995) stands as a charming entry in the switched-identity comedy genre, starring Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen at the height of their child acting careers. The film cleverly reworks elements from The Parent Trap (1961) and **Trading Places** (1983), following two identical-looking girls from different social backgrounds who meet by chance and scheme to unite a wealthy widower with a kind-hearted orphanage worker. The Olsen twins showcase their signature dynamic, with each playing distinctly different characters - the street-smart orphan Amanda and privileged Alyssa.

sections.content: The film follows a rich tradition of family-focused identity swap comedies from the 1990s, including **Big** (1988) and **Vice Versa** (1988). What sets **It Takes Two** apart is its wholesome approach to class differences and found family, themes that would later appear in films like **Annie** (1999) and **The Princess Diaries** (2001). The chemistry between Steve Guttenberg and Kirstie Alley provides the emotional anchor for the adult storyline, while the Olsen twins deliver performances that helped establish them as the defining child stars of the decade.

Director Andy Tennant, who would later helm **Sweet Home Alabama** (2002) and **Hitch** (2005), brings a light touch to the material that prevents it from becoming overly saccharine. The film's success helped pave the way for other family-friendly identity comedies like **Model Behavior** (2000) and **The Lizzie McGuire Movie** (2003), while maintaining its own distinct charm through its dual-protagonist structure and emphasis on creating unconventional families. sections.content: **It Takes Two** marked a pivotal moment in the Olsen twins' filmography, coming between their successful TV series **Two of a Kind** (1998) and direct-to-video empire that included titles like **Billboard Dad** (1998) and **Passport to Paris** (1999). The film demonstrates their ability to carry a theatrical release, something few child TV stars managed in the 1990s. Their natural rapport and ability to play distinct characters proved they were more than just sitcom actors, setting the stage for their later success as producers and fashion entrepreneurs.
